verdict.reasoning: The diff removes the case-insensitive standalone `failed` match and does not replace all genuine failure forms. Mixed-case outputs such as `Test Run Failed.`, `Failed: 1`, `Failed to compile.`, and `go vet failed` match none of the new patterns, so they can be missed when success text is also present. Some listed examples, such as TAP `not ok` and make `Error 2`, were not caught by the removed pattern either, but the demonstrated regressions are sufficient to make the finding real.

The new stated-check regex matches the unqualified substring "tests failed" or "checks failed" without considering preceding negation or a zero count. Therefore phrases such as "no tests failed", "0 tests failed", and "none of the checks failed" are classified as failures. The added "zero failed" test does not cover this because its text is "Tests: 12 passed, 0 failed", which does not match that regex shape. This is a verifiable false positive in the behavior the diff is intended to correct.
The new count regex searches for a matching substring, so in "0 of 10 failed" it matches the trailing "10 failed" and incorrectly classifies evidence that reports zero failures as a failure.

The diff already pins failure-over-success precedence in several cases by combining the success signal `go test ./... exited 0` with explicit failure shapes and expecting exit 1. It also tests a failure shape without that success signal via the `go test FAIL line` case. Although the exact spellings `Failures: 0` and `0 failures` are not visible here, the evidence contains no repository-wide test search establishing their absence, and the claim that unspecified regex changes could silently alter behavior is speculative rather than a concrete defect introduced by this diff.

verdict.reasoning: The defect is real. `zeroFailures` permits up to two arbitrary `\w+` tokens between `0` and a failure term, so it removes substrings such as `0 passed 3 failed` and `0 Failed` from `Passed: 0 Failed: 3`. After removal, `hasFailureSignal` can miss the genuine nonzero failure count, while the remaining success wording may still satisfy a success pattern. Some listed examples may not independently produce exit 0, but the core fail-open parsing bug is directly present in the added regex.

The new detector misses several standard nonzero failure markers. Most clearly, after zeroFailures removes "Failures: 0" from a Maven/JUnit summary such as "Failures: 0, Errors: 1", no failurePatterns regex matches "Errors: 1". Likewise, the patterns do not match standalone "BUILD FAILURE", "FAILURES!", "# fail 1", "npm ERR!", or "error CS1002:". Because hasFailureSignal then returns false, accompanying success text can incorrectly make a failing receipt appear successful. These are concrete gaps in the expanded fail-closed parsing introduced by this diff.

The finding identifies only a linear-time regex pass over the input and explicitly says it matters only for multi-megabyte evidence. RE2 avoids catastrophic backtracking, and the diff provides no evidence that such input sizes are permitted or that this extra pass creates a material performance problem. This is speculative advisory commentary, not a verifiable defect requiring action before merge.

verdict.reasoning: The new regex permits its match to begin at any space, so in "worker 0 failed" it matches and removes the substring " 0 failed" without understanding that 0 identifies the worker rather than a failure count. This also removes the only failure signal from analogous shard/job labels, allowing an accompanying success signal to pass the receipt incorrectly.

The diff removes the prior case-insensitive `\bFAIL\b` pattern and replaces it with an uppercase-only `FAIL` pattern plus lowercase `fail` patterns that require a nonzero count. Consequently status verdicts such as `Result: Fail`, `lint: fail`, and `build fail` match no failure pattern. If the same receipt contains a success signal such as `go test ./... ok`, it can be accepted despite the explicit failure verdict. This is a concrete regression from the base behavior and contradicts the stated fail-closed intent.

The new exit-status regex only matches `exit`, `exited`, `exit code`, or `exit status` followed directly by whitespace and a nonzero number. It does not match the listed colon, `with code/status`, equals-sign, or `return code` forms. Since the diff claims tool failure shapes are detected fail-closed, these common unmatched forms can be accepted when a separate success signal is present. The finding is concrete and directly verifiable from the regex.

The new neutralizer only matches count-first forms beginning with 0/no/none, so common label-first success summaries such as "Failed: 0" and "failed=0" remain intact and are then caught by the unconditional case-insensitive `failed` pattern. CRLF is also mishandled: under multiline mode `$` matches before `\n`, but the intervening `\r` is not an allowed trailing delimiter, so a line ending in "0 failed\r\n" is not neutralized. These passing outputs therefore produce a false failure signal.

The new regexes verifiably overmatch these examples. `2 error paths` matches the count-plus-`error` pattern; `fail2ban` matches `\bfail... [1-9]` because whitespace and punctuation are optional and no trailing boundary follows the digit; and `1 fail-over test` matches the `1 fail\b` pattern because `-` creates a word boundary. Thus non-failure prose can make `hasFailureSignal` return true and reject otherwise passing evidence.

The regex only neutralizes zero-failure phrases when `failed` is followed by end-of-line or one of `,;.)!`. Therefore `0 failed in 1s` and `0 failed (cached)` remain unchanged, after which the case-insensitive `\bfailed\b` pattern marks them as failures. This is a verifiable fail-closed false positive introduced by the diff.

verdict.reasoning: The finding is correct. The zero-count label alternative includes `[ \t]\w+=` in its terminating capture, so matching `failed=0 errors=3` consumes `failed=0 errors=`. `ReplaceAllString(text, "${1} ")` then removes that entire span (group 1 is unmatched for this alternative), leaving only `3`, which no failure pattern recognizes. The same issue hides `exit=1`. This creates a real fail-open regression.

The finding is correct. In ANSI-colored output such as "\u001b[31mFAIL\u001b[0m", the character immediately preceding "FAIL" is the word character "m". Therefore the leading `\b` in the relevant `FAIL`, `Fail`, and `failed` patterns does not match. No ANSI stripping is shown, so absent another failure token, a separate success signal can cause failed output to be accepted as passing.

The new regexes misclassify all cited passing summaries. `# fail 0` and `ℹ fail 0` match the fail-verdict rule because a digit is accepted after `fail`; `0 fail` matches the line-ending `fail` rule. `zeroFailures` neutralizes neither whitespace-separated `fail 0` nor singular `0 fail`, so `hasFailureSignal` returns true for these legitimate zero-failure outputs.

The finding identifies concrete regex gaps. In particular, the `rc` alternative accepts zero whitespace before the numeric status, so `v1.0.0-rc1` matches as a failure. Also, `^not ok`, bare `exited with 1`, `exit code was 1`, `TypeError:`, `N errors and M warnings`, and ctest's `0 tests failed out of 5` are not correctly handled by the shown patterns. Although several are uncommon formats, they are verifiable false-positive or false-negative cases in failure detection.

The diff does not claim exhaustive recognition of every tool output, and no supplied specification requires these particular shapes in this change. The new verdict regex `\b[Ff]ail\b[ \t]*([^ \ta-zA-Z\r\n(-]|\r?$)` treats both `/` and `.` after `fail` as failure punctuation. Therefore passing output such as `=== RUN TestX/fail` or `✓ src/fail.test.ts` matches `failurePatterns`; `hasFailureSignal` returns true and prevents a successful exit code even when a success signal is present. Neither zero-value neutralizer removes these paths.

verdict.reasoning: The new case-sensitive uppercase pattern catches only `FAIL`, while the mixed-case verdict regex explicitly excludes a following letter, `(`, `/`, `.`, or `-`. Thus forms such as `Result: Fail because timeout`, `lint: fail (3 warnings)`, and `build: Fail/timeout` match no failure pattern. If the same text contains a success signal, `parseFreeform` incorrectly returns exit code 0. The previous `(?i)\bFAIL\b` pattern caught all these forms, so this is a verifiable fail-open regression and contradicts the comment that punctuated fail verdicts count.

The newline case is a real regression: the old exit-code pattern used `\s+`, so `exit code\n1` was a failure signal, while the new pattern permits only spaces or tabs around the separator and number. In a receipt containing a success signal elsewhere, that nonzero exit can now be missed and the receipt accepted. `FAIL 0` and `error: 0` are intentionally neutralized zero-count labels, but the first example independently establishes the defect.

verdict.reasoning: The diff’s case-insensitive proseFail substitution runs before failurePatterns and removes phrases such as "FAIL on", "FAIL when", "did fail", and "does fail". This can erase genuine failure reports, including uppercase FAIL verdicts that the adjacent comment says must count, before the uppercase FAIL and generic fail patterns inspect them. If the same receipt contains a success signal, hasFailureSignal then returns false and parseFreeform incorrectly assigns exit code 0. The proposed examples therefore expose a concrete fail-open regression, although "will FAIL" alone may be an intentionally exempted hypothetical.

The regex intentionally neutralizes zero-count failure labels, including `failed 0` and `FAILED 0`, as documented by the adjacent comment. `FAILED 0` ordinarily reports zero failures, while `Build failed 0` is ambiguous and no concrete tool output or specified invariant establishes that it must remain a failure. Also, neutralization alone does not make the receipt pass; `parseFreeform` still requires an independent success signal. The finding therefore treats an intentional behavior change as a defect without verifiable evidence.
